b.v: Today's goal

v: Name the five tasks clients hand over most
Write what you will and will not do
Price by the hour or by the month, and know why

b.v: About 20 minutes. Keep a notebook and write your own list as you read.

A virtual assistant is not a person who does everything. A virtual assistant is a person who takes repeated, boring, time-eating tasks off someone else's desk and does them the same way every time. Clients pay for reliability, not for talent.
1) The work that gets delegated
Almost all beginner work is one of these five. Learn them well and you will always have something to sell.

v: Inbox: sorting, replying to routine mail, following up unpaid invoices
Calendar: booking meetings, reminders, avoiding double bookings
Data: moving information from one place to another without errors
Research: finding suppliers, prices, contact details, and writing a short summary
Reporting: a weekly or monthly update the client can read in two minutes

b.v: 2) Write your scope before you need it
A one-page scope protects you from the client who slowly hands you their whole business. Write it once, send it with your rate, and point at it when something new appears.

@Scope of work, one page
What I do: inbox triage twice a day, calendar booking, weekly order sheet update, Monday summary report.
Hours: up to 20 per week, Monday to Friday, 10 am to 6 pm Pakistan time.
What I do not do: phone calls to your customers, social media replies, bank payments, anything needing your password.
Response time: within 2 working hours.
Rate: agreed monthly, invoiced on the 1st, paid within 7 days.
3) Hourly or monthly
Hourly is safer at the start because you do not yet know how long things take. Monthly is better once the work is steady, because the client stops counting and you stop worrying.

v: Hourly: new client, unclear work, or work that comes in waves
Monthly retainer: same tasks every week, agreed hours, predictable
Per task: small clear jobs such as a cleaned sheet or a research list

b.v: Do not agree to be available all day for a small monthly amount. Unlimited availability is the most common reason new assistants burn out in the third month and quit badly, losing the reference they needed.
Practice

Write your one-page scope with the five tasks above, keeping only the ones you can do confidently. Then write the sentence that lists what you do not do. Keep this page; you will send it to your first client.

day-2.t: Day 2 — The tool stack that earns its place

b.v: Today's goal

v: Choose five tools, not fifteen
Set up one shared folder structure the client can follow
Learn the sharing settings that protect the client

b.v: About 25 minutes. Create the accounts you are missing; most of these have free plans.
Clients do not pay for the tools you know. They pay because you can be handed a messy account and make it work. Still, a small reliable set of tools makes you look organised from the first day.
1) Five tools cover almost every beginner job
Pick one from each row and learn it properly. A deep knowledge of one spreadsheet beats a shallow knowledge of six apps.

v: Communication: email and a chat app the client already uses
Documents: a shared drive folder with a clear structure
Calendar: one calendar with the client, and one for yourself
Spreadsheets: one tool, formulas and filters learned well
Tasks: a simple list the client can see, not a system only you understand

b.v: 2) A folder structure the client can follow
Clients lose files when folders are named by date or by mood. Use numbers and short names, and never rename the client's existing folders without asking.

Set up the shared folder:|01 Inbox — files sent to me, unprocessed|02 Working — files I am working on now|03 Done — finished work, by month|04 Reference — templates, logins list, brand files|05 Reports — weekly and monthly summaries
3) Sharing settings that keep you safe
Share only the folder the client needs, and check the link setting before you send it. A public link to a client's customer list is a serious problem, even by accident.

v: Share with the client's email, not with anyone who has the link
Give edit rights only to people who must edit
Check the sharing list every month and remove people who left
Never store passwords in a shared document; use a password manager

b.v: Do not keep the client's files in your personal drive after the job ends. Download what you need for your records, then remove your access, and say that you did.
Practice

Create the five folders in your own drive today, with one practice file in each, and check the sharing settings. Then pick the one tool you are weakest at and book thirty minutes this week to learn it.

day-3.t: Day 3 — Inbox management that clients notice

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set up labels and three sorting rules
Write saved replies for the five most common emails
Use a daily two-pass system that takes 30 minutes

b.v: About 25 minutes. Ask the client for read-only access first, not full control.
An inbox is the first place a client sees your work. When they open it in the evening and only five emails need them, they feel the value immediately. That feeling is what renews your contract.
1) Sort into five buckets, no more
Fewer labels get used. More labels get ignored. Five is enough for almost any small business.

v: Action — the client must decide or sign something
Reply — I can answer this myself with a saved reply
Waiting — I have replied and I am waiting for someone
Reference — useful later, no action
Archive — done, out of the inbox

b.v: 2) Three rules that do most of the work
Set filters so the obvious mail is already sorted when you arrive. Never auto-delete anything a client might need.

Set the rules:|Rule 1: mail from the client's own team goes to Action|Rule 2: mail with invoice or receipt in the subject goes to Reference|Rule 3: newsletters and notifications skip the inbox and get a label|Test each rule on old mail before switching it on
3) Saved replies for the five common emails
Write them once in the client's voice, with a blank for the name. Read before sending: a reply that says Dear [Name] is worse than no reply.

@Saved replies
1. Thank you for your email. I have passed this to [client] and you will hear back today.
2. Attached is the invoice you asked for. Payment details are on the last page.
3. We have received your order and it will be dispatched within two working days.
4. Thank you for following up. I am checking with our supplier and will confirm by tomorrow.
5. This is not something we handle, but I can point you to [name] who does.
Do not send a reply in the client's name that promises a price, a discount or a delivery date you were not given. When in doubt, draft it and leave it for the client to send.
Practice
Create the five labels in your own inbox and sort your last fifty emails into them. Time yourself. Then write two saved replies in your own words for the messages you receive most.

day-4.t: Day 4 — Calendar management without double bookings

b.v: Today's goal

v: Book a meeting correctly in one pass
Handle time zones without mistakes
Protect focus time and travel time

b.v: About 20 minutes. Use two calendars with different colours so you can see conflicts.
A missed meeting is not a small error. It makes the client look bad in front of their customer, and it is the fastest way to lose a retainer. Calendar work is small, repeated and unforgiving.
1) The booking checklist
Run the same checklist for every meeting. It takes forty seconds and prevents almost every mistake.

Book a meeting:|Check the client's calendar for the exact slot, in their time zone|Check travel time if the meeting is in person|Add the guest, with the correct email address|Write a clear title, for example Order review with Ali, not Meeting|Add the video link or address and the phone number|Add an agenda in the description, even one line|Send the invite and confirm the guest accepted
2) Time zones, in plain words

Never write a time without the city. Pakistan Standard Time is UTC+5, and clients in London, Dubai and New York are all different distances from it. Put the city in the invite and let the calendar convert.

v: Good: 4:00 pm PKT / 11:00 am London
Bad: 4 pm my time
Good: 9:30 am Dubai / 10:30 am Karachi
Check the daylight saving change twice a year for Europe and North America

b.v: 3) Protect blocks the client cannot see
Add your own focus time and prayer breaks to your calendar, and tell the client in week one that these blocks exist. It is much easier than explaining later.
Do not accept a meeting on the client's behalf without checking their calendar first, even if the time looks free in the email thread. Clients often have private blocks that are not shared with you.
Practice
Create one event in your own calendar with the full checklist: title, guest, video link, agenda, and the time written with both cities. Then add two recurring blocks for focus time and breaks.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Meeting notes people actually read

b.v: Today's goal

v: Capture decisions, not conversation
Use one notes format every time
Send the notes within two hours

b.v: About 20 minutes. Use the notes from your last real meeting, or a video call you can watch.
A transcript is not notes. A client does not want what everyone said. They want what was decided, who does what, and by when. That version gets read and forwarded; the long one gets ignored.
1) Four sections in a fixed order
Same order every time, so a client can find the action list without reading the rest.

v: Attendees and date
Decisions — one line each, no discussion
Actions — who, what, by when
Open questions — the things nobody answered

b.v: 2) A full template
Copy this into a document and reuse it. Keep the notes under one page.

@Meeting notes
Meeting: Weekly order review
Date: 12 March, 4:00 pm PKT
Present: Ali (client), Sana (accounts), me

DECISIONS
1. Supplier B will be dropped from April.
2. Free delivery threshold stays at Rs 2,500 for now.

ACTIONS
- Sana: send March supplier totals by 14 March
- Me: update the order sheet with the new supplier list by 13 March
- Ali: confirm the April price list before the next call

OPEN QUESTIONS
1. Who approves refunds above Rs 5,000 when Ali is travelling?
3) Send within two hours
Notes sent the same day feel like service. Notes sent next week feel like homework. Send them to the attendees, with the action list repeated at the top of the email.
Do not record a call without telling everyone in it. In many countries that is illegal, and even where it is allowed, a client who finds out later will not trust you again.
Practice
Write notes for a meeting you attended this week using the template. Send them to one person who was there and ask whether the actions are right.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Data entry with accuracy habits

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build a two-check routine for every batch
Use formats and drop-downs to stop errors at the source
Report errors honestly instead of hiding them

b.v: About 25 minutes. Use any messy list of names, numbers or orders you can find.
Clients forgive slow. They do not forgive wrong. One mistyped phone number can cost a shop a customer, and one wrong total makes the whole sheet untrustworthy.
1) Enter, then check twice, differently
The second check must use a different method from the first, or your eyes repeat the same mistake. Compare totals, sort, and spot-check the ends.

Batch check:|Enter the data in one pass without stopping to fix anything|Count the rows in the source and in your sheet, and match them|Compare the total of one money column against the source total|Sort by the name column and look for duplicates|Spot-check the first five, the last five and five at random|Write the row count and the total at the top of the sheet
2) Stop errors before they happen
Formatting is not decoration. It is error prevention. A date column set to text will accept 31 February; a drop-down will not accept a misspelled city.

v: Set the date column to a real date format, not text
Use a drop-down for city, item and status columns
Use number format for money, with two decimals
Lock the header row and freeze it
Colour the cells that need checking, then remove the colour before delivery

b.v: 3) When you find your own mistake
Say it immediately, with the fix and the impact. A small honest correction builds more trust than a perfect record ever could.

@Correction message
I found an error in the batch I sent yesterday: rows 240 to 255 had the wrong city, Lahore instead of Multan. I have corrected them and re-checked the totals; the total is unchanged. The corrected file is attached. Sorry for the extra check on your side.
Do not quietly fix an error you already reported as done, and do not blame the source file. Clients remember how you behaved after a mistake far longer than they remember the mistake.
Practice
Take a list of twenty rows and enter it twice, using two different methods, then compare. Write down how many differences you found. That number is why the double check exists.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Research tasks with a usable answer

b.v: Today's goal

v: Turn a vague request into a clear research brief
Find and verify information quickly
Deliver a one-page answer, not a folder of links

b.v: About 25 minutes. Pick a real question a shop owner you know would ask.
Anybody can paste ten links. A client pays for the short answer: these three suppliers, these prices, this is the catch. Research is mostly about deciding what to leave out.
1) Write the brief back before you start
Send three lines to confirm what is needed. This one message prevents a whole day of work on the wrong question.

v: What decision will you make with this?
Which cities, brands or price ranges count?
Do you want five options with detail, or twenty with none?

b.v: 2) A research sheet with four columns
Keep every source and every price on one sheet, so you can answer a follow-up question without starting again.

@Research sheet columns
Option | What it is | Price and date checked | Source link | Note (delivery, minimum order, risk)
3) Verify before you recommend
Prices and contact details go out of date fast. Check the date on the page, and phone or message one supplier to confirm before you put a number in front of a client.

v: Open the source page, do not trust the search result snippet
Write the date you checked next to every price
Confirm one option directly, so at least one is proven
Say clearly which numbers are confirmed and which are from a website

b.v: Do not present an old price as today's price, and do not hide a catch such as a minimum order or a delivery charge. One surprise after the client acts on your research ends the relationship.
Practice
Take one real question, write the brief back, and produce a one-page answer with five options, prices with dates, and one recommendation with a reason.

day-8.t: Day 8 — The weekly report that renews contracts

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write a weekly update the client reads in two minutes
Show finished work, next week and anything stuck
Use it to raise problems early

b.v: About 20 minutes. Write last week's report even if you have no client yet; it becomes your sample.

Clients do not see your work. They see their inbox and their own stress. A short report every week is the cheapest way to prove you are worth the money, and it is the first thing they miss when you stop.
1) Four sections, fixed length
Keep the whole thing under 250 words. Long reports get skimmed, and skimmed reports get forgotten.

v: Done this week — three to five lines, with numbers
Next week — what you will do, in order
Stuck or waiting — what you need from the client, with a date
One number to watch — a small measure that shows progress

b.v: 2) A full example
Notice that every line has a number or a name, and that the stuck item is stated plainly, with a date.

@Weekly report, week of 10 March
DONE
- Cleared the inbox to zero twice a day, 84 emails handled, 9 sent to you for a decision.
- Updated the order sheet daily; 412 orders entered and checked.
- Booked 6 meetings, no double bookings.

NEXT WEEK
- Rebuild the supplier tab with the April list.
- Send the March summary on the 1st.

STUCK
- I need the April price list from you before Wednesday, otherwise the March summary uses old prices.

NUMBER TO WATCH
- Orders entered per hour went from 38 to 51 after the drop-down change.
3) Use it to raise bad news early
The Stuck section is where you tell the client something is late, missing or wrong. Put it there every week, even when it is empty, so that a filled section is normal and not a crisis.
Do not hide a delay hoping to fix it before anyone notices. The report exists so the client hears it from you first, with a plan, instead of from their customer.
Practice
Write this week's report now using the four sections and at least three numbers. Save it as a template so future weeks take ten minutes.

day-9.t: Day 9 — Time zones, confidentiality and NDAs

b.v: Today's goal

v: Work across time zones without missed handovers
Understand what confidentiality means in daily practice
Read an NDA before you sign it

b.v: About 20 minutes. Check the time difference for your main client and write it on a sticky note.

A client hands you their customer list, their prices and their problems. That trust is the whole business. Time zones are the daily practical side of the same thing: being where you said you would be.
1) Time zone discipline
Write times with the city, keep one world clock on your phone, and agree a handover time in writing.

v: Agree one overlap window of two hours a day when both of you are online
Write the client's time zone in your calendar, not yours
Send an end-of-day note before you log off, so morning starts with answers
Check daylight saving changes in March and October for Europe and North America

b.v: 2) Confidentiality in daily practice
An NDA is a non-disclosure agreement: a promise not to share the client's private information. You do not need a lawyer to follow the basics, and most of them are habits, not rules.

v: Use the client's own accounts, not your personal email, for their mail
Never forward customer lists to your personal address to work on later
Do not name the client or show their data in your portfolio without written permission
Blur or replace real names and numbers in every screenshot you share
Do not discuss one client's business with another

b.v: 3) Before you sign
Read the whole document once, then check four things. If any is unclear, ask in writing before signing — a good client expects the question.

Check an NDA:|What exactly is confidential, and for how long|Whether you may show the work as a sample, and how|Whether you can work for competitors|Which country's law applies and how disputes are handled
Do not sign an NDA that forbids all similar work for years, or one that makes you personally liable for unlimited losses. Ask for a change, or walk away; there is always another client.
Practice
Write your own one-paragraph confidentiality promise you can send to clients who have no NDA. Then note the overlap window you will offer your next client, with both cities named.

day-10.t: Day 10 — Invoicing, getting paid, and raising your rate

b.v: Today's goal

v: Send an invoice that gets paid on time
Know your payout options from Pakistan
Ask for a higher rate without losing the client

b.v: About 25 minutes. Payout options and fees change, so check the current details with your bank and your platform.
Good work with bad paperwork is a hobby. You need an invoice, a payment route and a record of everything you sent. Then you need to raise your rate, or you will be busy and poor at the same time.
1) The invoice that gets paid
An invoice is a request for money with enough detail that nobody has to ask a question. Send it the same day the month ends, not when you remember.

v: Invoice number and date, plus the payment due date
Client name and your name, with your address
Line items: what, which month, hours or quantity, rate
Total, and the currency, written clearly
Payment details, and a note on who pays the transfer fee

b.v:
@Invoice
Invoice 2026-03
From: Ayesha Khan, Karachi
To: Northline Traders

1. Inbox and calendar support, March, 60 hours at agreed rate
2. Weekly reports, 4 reports
3. Supplier sheet rebuild, one-time

Total due: Rs (agreed amount)
Due date: 7 April
Send to: (account name, account number, bank or wallet)

Please send the transfer reference once paid so I can mark it in my records.
2) Getting paid from Pakistan
Ask how the client pays before the first day of work, not after the first month. Then confirm what your side receives after fees, so there are no surprises.

v: Freelance platforms pay out through their own supported methods; check what is available to Pakistan at the time of writing
Bank transfer in foreign currency: ask your bank about the receiving charge and the conversion rate
Wallets such as Payoneer: confirm the fee and the withdrawal time before you rely on it
Local wallets such as JazzCash and Easypaisa suit local clients, not foreign ones
Keep every invoice, payment screenshot and bank credit in one folder for tax time

b.v: Do not start work for a new client without agreeing the currency, the payment date and who pays the transfer fee. Arguments about money after the work is done are almost never won, only survived.
3) Raising your rate
Raise it on a schedule, not in a bad mood. Give notice, give a reason, and make it easy to say yes.

@Rate increase message
Thank you for a good six months — the order sheet now runs without the month-end panic.

From 1 May my rate will be (new rate). This reflects the reporting work I took on in February and the extra hours the second shop added.

Nothing changes before 1 May, and I am happy to keep the current rate until then. If the new rate does not work for you, tell me and we can look at reducing the scope instead.
Practice
Create your invoice template with every field above, and write your rate increase message. Then put a date in your calendar four months from now to review your rate.
